# What Investors Fund in Media Now

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-investors-fund-in-media-now/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-13 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Investors fund media businesses with owned audiences that pay, proprietary products those audiences need, and revenue that does not depend on a platform. Reach is the raw material, not the asset. With search traffic to publishers down a third and only 17% of people paying for online news, the evidence that counts is repeat behaviour: paid conversion, renewal, sponsor renewal and signed licensing.

Investors fund media businesses with owned audiences that pay, proprietary products those audiences need, and revenue that does not depend on a platform. Reach is the raw material, not the asset. The 2026 data explains why: Google organic search traffic to more than 2,500 publisher sites fell 33% in a year, the share of people paying for online news held at about 17% across 20 countries, and media leaders expect AI licensing to be a minor contribution at best.

*This is commercial advisory, not investment advice.*

## What stopped getting funded

Ad-supported reach was fundable when traffic was cheap and advertisers paid by volume. Neither holds now. Platforms changed their terms, programmatic rates fell, and the cost of acquiring attention rose.

The traffic data is stark. The Reuters Institute's 2026 trends report cites Chartbeat data showing Google organic search traffic to more than 2,500 news sites fell by a third globally, and by 38% in the US, between November 2024 and November 2025. Referrals from Facebook fell 43% and from X 46% over roughly three years. Publishers surveyed expect search traffic to fall by more than 40% over the next three years. The Reuters Institute's Digital News Report 2026 found social and video networks are now the most used way to reach online news, at 54% of respondents, ahead of news organisations' own sites and apps at 51%.

Venture money has followed. Carta's first-half 2026 data shows capital raised by advertising technology companies on its platform falling from $335 million to $65 million year on year.

Investors who backed that model carry the scars. When a media founder leads with page views and impressions, the first reaction is not interest. It is pattern recognition.

That does not mean media is unfundable. It means the thing being funded has changed. [Raise against evidence, not narrative](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/) says raise on what users have done. In media, the narrative is almost always growth in attention. The evidence is growth in money from people who chose to pay.

## What gets funded

Five models attract capital in media today. Most funded companies combine two or three.

| Model | What proves it | The main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Owned audience that pays | Free-to-paid conversion and renewal after the first term | A low ceiling on willingness to pay |
| Proprietary data or research for B2B buyers | Annual contracts, daily use, low churn | Buyers build or buy it elsewhere |
| Licensing | Signed agreements with terms | Uneven demand; many publishers get no offer |
| Events and community with margins | Sponsor renewal, ticket revenue, a visible cost base | Break-even events that look like growth |
| Tooling or software on the audience | Software margins attached to distribution | Becoming a software company without the team |

**Owned audience with demonstrated willingness to pay.** Paid subscriptions, memberships, premium tiers. The proof is not the list size; it is the conversion from free to paid and the renewal after the first term. The ceiling is real: the Digital News Report 2026 found the share paying for online news across its 20-country basket was 17%, against 18% in 2025, with Norway at 40% and the UK at 10%. Even large publishers are not immune. The same report notes USA Today Co. reported a 30% drop in total subscribers during 2025. [Membership is the job](https://lowob.com/research/membership-is-the-job/) covers how to give paying members a reason to stay.

**Proprietary data or research that B2B buyers pay for.** Market maps, benchmarks, deal data, rankings, surveys. Buyers put these in budgets, sign annual contracts, and rarely churn if the data is used daily.

**Licensing.** Syndication, republication, archive access, and now content licensing to AI developers. The AI licensing market is real, but uneven: terms vary widely, demand favours depth and originality, and many publishers get no offer at all. The Reuters Institute's survey of 280 media leaders found 20% expect AI-related revenue to be substantial, 49% expect a minor contribution, and another 20%, mostly local publishers, public broadcasters and those in smaller countries, expect none. Treat it as upside, not a plan.

**Events and community with margins.** Not a conference that breaks even. A programme with sponsor renewal, ticket revenue, and a cost base you can show. Events are rising as a priority: 54% of media leaders in the Reuters Institute survey named them as increasingly important, behind subscription and membership at 76%.

**Tooling or software layered on the audience.** Directories, calculators, job boards, deal-flow tools, databases. Software margins attached to a distribution advantage.

## The evidence that counts

Most media decks lead with audience growth charts. Investors look past them to a short set of figures that describe whether the business works.

| Evidence | What it proves |
| --- | --- |
| Paid conversion rate | The audience values the product enough to pay |
| Renewal rate | They still value it after they have had it |
| Revenue per subscriber | The economics of one relationship |
| Sponsor renewal rate | Advertisers got results, not just impressions |
| Signed licensing agreements | A third party has valued the content in writing |
| Share of revenue not platform-dependent | What survives a policy change |

Notice that every line is about repeat behaviour. One-off revenue tells an investor you can sell. Repeat revenue tells them you have built something. Report retention the way a subscription business does: our explainers on [net revenue retention](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-net-revenue-retention/) and [NRR vs GRR](https://lowob.com/research/nrr-vs-grr/) cover which number to show.

If you cannot populate this table yet, that is your pre-raise work. [Your first ten sponsors are design partners](https://lowob.com/research/your-first-ten-sponsors-are-design-partners/) covers the media version of design partners: your first paying cohort and your first renewing sponsors.

> A sponsor buys next quarter. An investor buys the next five years.

## Alternatives to venture capital

Venture suits a small share of media businesses: those with a software layer, a large addressable B2B market, or a data product that compounds. For many others, venture terms are a poor fit for the growth rate media can deliver.

| Route | Suits | What it needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Venture | Software layer, large B2B market, compounding data | A path to venture-scale growth |
| Revenue-based finance | Predictable subscription or sponsorship income | Steady monthly revenue to repay from |
| Strategic investors | Audience or data a larger company wants | Clarity on what they get and the exit path |
| Partnerships | A product line a sponsor or platform will fund | Terms on exclusivity or first access |
| Bootstrapping | Profitable niches | Patience; the business stays sellable at any point |

Each route needs the same evidence as venture. The buyer changes, the proof does not.

## Running the raise

[Run the round like a sales process](https://lowob.com/research/run-the-round-like-a-sales-process/) covers the method. Media founders often skip this because they are used to pitching sponsors, which is a different sale.

A sponsor buys next quarter. An investor buys the next five years. The materials need to show the model, not the audience. The data room needs the claims register from [One truth, three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/), the evidence table above, and the cohort behaviour behind it. Our [Build Order for media and publishing](https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-media-and-publishing/) covers how to keep those records as routine.

The most common gap I see is a strong audience and no revenue story. Fix the revenue story first. It changes who you can talk to and what they will offer.

## lowob takeaways

- **Reach is raw material, not the asset.** Platform traffic is falling and investors know it.
- **Lead with repeat behaviour.** Conversion, renewal, sponsor renewal and signed licences.
- **Treat AI licensing as upside.** Most media leaders expect a minor contribution or none.
- **Compare routes before choosing venture.** Each needs the same evidence; the terms differ.

## Common questions

### What kind of media companies do investors fund today?

Businesses with owned audiences that pay, proprietary data or research B2B buyers pay for, licensing, events and community with margins, and software layered on the audience. Most funded companies combine two or three.

### What metrics do investors look for in a media startup?

Paid conversion rate, renewal rate, revenue per subscriber, sponsor renewal rate, signed licensing agreements, and the share of revenue not dependent on platforms. Every line is about repeat behaviour.

### Is AI content licensing a reliable revenue stream for publishers?

Not yet. In the Reuters Institute's 2026 survey of 280 media leaders, 20% expected substantial AI revenue, 49% a minor contribution and 20% none. Treat it as upside, not a plan.

### How many people pay for online news?

About 17% across the Reuters Institute's 20-country basket in 2026, against 18% in 2025, with wide variation: 40% in Norway and 10% in the UK.

## Sources and notes

- [Reuters Institute, Journalism, media and technology trends and predictions 2026](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/journalism-media-and-technology-trends-and-predictions-2026), 12 January 2026. Strategic sample of 280 digital leaders in 51 countries, plus Chartbeat traffic data; not representative of all publishers.
- [Reuters Institute, Digital News Report 2026: executive summary](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2026/dnr-executive-summary), 16 June 2026. Online survey of 97,520 people across markets, about 2,000 per market; online samples under-represent offline users.
- [Carta, The venture market shifted in the first half of the year](https://carta.com/data/newsletter-venture-market-shifted-first-half/), 8 July 2026. Carta platform data; advertising technology category is Carta's.
